title: Better training called for to subdue frenzied patients:
article: A judge has urged continued training for emergency workers so they know how to deal with psychiatric patients who explode in sometimes lethal frenzies of rage.

Two burly police officers and a psychiatric nurse could barely subdue Kasim Cakmak on May 11, 2001, when they tried to take him from the downtown mental health outpatient clinic to Alberta Hospital Edmonton.

The 37-year-old paranoid schizophrenic had been following women in the building, muttering to himself, yelling and acting aggressively, so a psychiatrist declared him an involuntary patient who could be treated against his will.
But he went wild when police approached with psychiatric nurse Mike Brohman, thrashing, screaming and lashing out, Brohman told a fatality inquiry last year.
Officers tried pepper spray, but Brohman said he was hit by most of the liquid because Cakmak was flailing, kicking and "screaming like Tarzan."
It took about five minutes to force him face down on the ground with his hands cuffed behind his back.
"The intensity of the outburst, I have never seen that strength, ever," said Brohman, who has worked 16 years as a psychiatric nurse.
"They were trying to contain him and he was bucking them off like (at) a rodeo. I could see that they weren't able to hold him and were panicking."
Ninety seconds later, Brohman noticed that Cakmak's face was blue. Police removed the handcuffs and rolled him on to his back. There was no pulse. He had stopped breathing.
Cakmak died of excited delirium, a rare condition affecting psychiatric patients and cocaine users who become so agitated an overpowering adrenaline rush stops their heart.
In a fatality inquiry report released Thursday, provincial court judge Darlene Wong recommended police and emergency services continue research and training to help staff recognize this condition.
The judge seemed satisfied with the work done by Edmonton police, which began giving officers an information package on the subject in October 2001.
"If other police services and emergency services are not undertaking this kind of research and training, it would seem to be important to consider to do so," says the report, completed in April.
As a result of Cakmak's death, police developed a program on dealing with excited delirium given to all officers last spring during safety training, police spokeswoman Annette Bidniak said.
It will be part of the regular training, she said.
"This is one of those things that happens rarely, but is devastating for everyone involved."
Dr. Sunil Sookram, medical officer for the emergency response department, said paramedics are already taught how to handle violent people, including someone in such an extreme state.
Options include defusing the situation verbally, using sedatives and controlling the patient with arm restraints, he said.
